supply_chain_regulations.title: Policy
supply_chain_regulations.description: Establishes the policy that the United States Government must improve its efforts to identify, deter, protect against, detect, and respond to cyber threats. Recognizes that incremental improvements will not provide the necessary security and that bold changes and significant investments are needed. The Federal Government must lead by example and use its purchasing power to drive supply chain security improvements across the private sector.
requirements: Federal Government must improve cybersecurity posture
Private sector must adapt to the continuously changing threat environment
Prevention, detection, assessment, and remediation of cyber incidents is a top priority
Federal Government procurement power to be used to drive security improvements
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: All Federal agencies and their technology suppliers. Sets the policy direction for subsequent sections.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: Office of Management and Budget (OMB) oversees implementation. Agency heads responsible for compliance.

framework_mappings.SLSA: General alignment with supply chain integrity goals

supply_chain_regulations.title: Removing Barriers to Sharing Threat Information
supply_chain_regulations.description: Requires federal agencies and their IT service providers to promptly share cyber threat and incident information. Removes contractual barriers that may prevent service providers from sharing threat data with CISA, FBI, and other agencies. Mandates that service provider contracts include provisions for collecting and preserving data relevant to cybersecurity event prevention, detection, response, and investigation.
requirements: IT service provider contracts must include threat information sharing provisions
Remove contractual barriers to sharing threat data with government
Service providers must share incident and threat data with CISA, FBI, and agency
Agencies must update contract requirements within 60 days of OMB guidance
Service providers must collect and preserve data relevant to cyber events
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: All Federal agency IT service provider contracts, including cloud service providers (FedRAMP authorized).
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: FAR Council updates acquisition regulations. OMB issues implementation guidance.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Modernizing Federal Government Cybersecurity
supply_chain_regulations.description: Directs Federal agencies to modernize their approach to cybersecurity by adopting Zero Trust Architecture, accelerating migration to secure cloud services, implementing multi-factor authentication, and encrypting data at rest and in transit. Sets specific timelines for agencies to adopt these technologies and report on progress. Emphasizes that cloud services can provide security capabilities that individual agencies cannot achieve on their own.
requirements: Adopt Zero Trust Architecture within agency networks
Accelerate migration to secure cloud services (FedRAMP authorized)
Deploy multi-factor authentication within 180 days for all users
Encrypt data at rest and in transit within 180 days
Adopt and use CISA's Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation (CDM) program
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: All Federal civilian executive branch agencies (FCEB). Encouraged for national security systems.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: OMB tracks implementation progress. Agency heads report to National Security Advisor.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Enhancing Software Supply Chain Security
supply_chain_regulations.description: The most impactful section for supply chain security. Directs NIST to publish guidelines for enhancing software supply chain security, including criteria for evaluating software security practices of developers and suppliers. Requires federal agencies to obtain a self-attestation from software producers that they comply with secure development practices. Establishes the requirement for SBOMs and mandates NIST to develop the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF).
requirements: NIST to publish guidelines on secure software development practices
Software producers must self-attest to compliance with secure development practices
SBOM must be provided for software sold to the Federal Government
Critical software to be defined and subject to enhanced security requirements
FAR/DFAR acquisition rules to be updated to enforce supply chain security
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: All software sold to the Federal Government, with enhanced requirements for 'critical software'.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: OMB memoranda (M-22-18, M-23-16) implement requirements. CISA maintains list of critical software categories.

supply_chain_regulations.title: SBOM Requirements for Federal Procurement
supply_chain_regulations.description: Specifically mandates that software producers provide an SBOM to federal agency purchasers. The SBOM must identify the components and their versions used in the software. NTIA (now CISA) is directed to publish minimum elements for SBOMs. This provision was the single most impactful policy driver for SBOM adoption, creating a market-wide demand signal for SBOM generation capabilities.
requirements: Software producers must provide SBOM to federal purchasers
SBOM must include minimum elements as defined by NTIA/CISA
SBOM must be machine-readable and in a standard format
SBOM generation must be automated as part of the development process
SBOM must cover direct and transitive dependencies
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: All software producers selling to the Federal Government.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: Federal acquisition regulations (FAR). Agencies must include SBOM requirements in procurement. OMB M-22-18 and M-23-16 provide implementation timelines.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Secure Software Development Attestation
supply_chain_regulations.description: Requires software producers to attest to conformity with secure software development practices as defined by NIST guidance (SSDF). The attestation must confirm that the producer follows documented security practices including source code security, build integrity, vulnerability management, and dependency management. This self-attestation regime enables scaled enforcement without requiring individual product certification.
requirements: Software producers must self-attest to compliance with SSDF practices
Attestation must be signed by a corporate officer or authorized representative
Attestation covers secure development lifecycle practices
Third-party assessment may be required for critical software
Attestation must be maintained and updated as practices evolve
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: All software producers selling to the Federal Government. OMB M-22-18 provides the attestation form (CISA Secure Software Development Attestation Form).
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: OMB M-22-18 and M-23-16. CISA maintains the attestation repository. False attestation may constitute fraud.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Critical Software Definition and Enhanced Security
supply_chain_regulations.description: Directs NIST and CISA to define 'critical software' categories that require enhanced security measures. Critical software includes software that runs with elevated privileges, controls access to data or operational technology, or performs functions critical to trust (e.g., network control, identity management, operating systems). Critical software is subject to more stringent security requirements and potentially third-party assessment.
requirements: NIST/CISA to define 'critical software' categories
Enhanced security measures apply to critical software
May require third-party security assessment instead of self-attestation
Immediate priority for implementing EO 14028 requirements
Agencies must identify critical software in use and apply enhanced protections
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: Software identified as 'critical' per NIST/CISA definition, including operating systems, hypervisors, identity management, network management, and operational technology software.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: CISA published critical software definition. Agencies must prioritize critical software compliance.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Cyber Safety Review Board (CSRB)
supply_chain_regulations.description: Establishes the Cyber Safety Review Board modeled after the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB). The CSRB reviews and assesses significant cyber incidents affecting Federal civilian government or non-Federal systems. The Board includes representatives from government agencies and private sector cybersecurity experts. It produces public reports with recommendations to improve cybersecurity, including supply chain security lessons learned.
requirements: Establish Cyber Safety Review Board with government and private sector members
Review significant cyber incidents affecting federal and private sector systems
Produce public reports with actionable recommendations
Initial review of the SolarWinds/SUNBURST supply chain attack
Board can convene after significant supply chain compromise events
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: Significant cyber incidents affecting Federal Government or critical infrastructure, including supply chain attacks.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: Secretary of Homeland Security convenes the Board. Recommendations are advisory, not binding.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Standardizing the Federal Government's Playbook for Responding to Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities and Incidents
supply_chain_regulations.description: Directs CISA to develop a standard set of operational procedures (playbook) for federal agencies to follow when responding to cybersecurity vulnerabilities and incidents on FCEB information systems. The playbook incorporates NIST standards and must be updated annually. It ensures consistent, comprehensive response across the Federal Government, particularly important for supply chain incidents that may affect multiple agencies simultaneously.
requirements: CISA to develop cybersecurity vulnerability and incident response playbook
Playbook must incorporate NIST standards and best practices
All FCEB agencies must adopt the playbook
Playbook must be reviewed and updated at least annually
Playbook must address supply chain incident coordination
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: All Federal civilian executive branch (FCEB) agencies. National security systems encouraged to adopt equivalent procedures.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: OMB oversight. CISA published the Federal Government Cybersecurity Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks in November 2021.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Improving Detection of Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities and Incidents on Federal Government Networks
supply_chain_regulations.description: Mandates improved endpoint detection and response (EDR) capabilities across Federal networks. Directs deployment of government-wide EDR solutions to support proactive detection, active cyber hunting, containment, remediation, and incident response. This section strengthens the ability to detect supply chain attacks that may manifest as anomalous behavior on endpoints rather than through traditional network-based detection.
requirements: Deploy Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) across FCEB agencies
Support proactive cyber threat hunting capabilities
Establish centralized visibility through CISA for cross-agency detection
Enable real-time detection and containment of cyber threats
Implement robust intra-governmental information sharing
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: All FCEB agencies and their managed endpoints.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: OMB sets deployment timelines. CISA provides technical requirements and oversight.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Improving the Federal Government's Investigative and Remediation Capabilities
supply_chain_regulations.description: Establishes requirements for logging, log retention, and log sharing across Federal agencies. Agencies must maintain logs required for investigating cybersecurity incidents and share them with CISA and FBI upon request. Standardized logging requirements ensure that when supply chain incidents occur, sufficient forensic data exists across all affected agencies to support investigation and attribution.
requirements: Agencies must maintain security logs per OMB guidance (M-21-31)
Logs must be retained for the period specified in OMB guidance
Logs must be shared with CISA and FBI for incident investigation
Logging must cover network, system, and application layers
Cloud service providers must provide equivalent logging capabilities
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: All FCEB agencies and their IT service providers, including cloud service providers.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: OMB M-21-31 (Improving the Federal Government's Investigative and Remediation Capabilities). Agencies must achieve compliance tiers within specified timelines.

supply_chain_regulations.title: National Security Systems
supply_chain_regulations.description: Requires the Secretary of Defense and the Director of National Intelligence to adopt requirements equivalent to the EO for National Security Systems (NSS) within 60 days. While NSS are not directly subject to the civilian EO provisions, this section ensures that the same supply chain security improvements apply to the most sensitive government systems. NSS-specific implementations may include additional classified requirements.
requirements: Adopt requirements equivalent to the EO for National Security Systems
Implementation within 60 days of the EO
Committee on National Security Systems (CNSS) to issue directives
May include additional classified requirements beyond civilian EO
Cross-domain information sharing where appropriate
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: National Security Systems across the Department of Defense and Intelligence Community.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: Secretary of Defense and Director of National Intelligence. CNSS directives.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Software Supply Chain Security Guidelines
supply_chain_regulations.description: Directs NIST to issue guidelines on software supply chain security practices, including criteria for evaluating the security practices of software developers and suppliers. These guidelines became NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF) and the NIST Secure Software Development Framework. The guidelines address the entire software development lifecycle from source code management through build, testing, distribution, and maintenance.
requirements: NIST to publish supply chain security guidelines within 6 months
Guidelines must address source code security and integrity
Guidelines must address build environment security
Guidelines must address vulnerability disclosure and management
Guidelines must address provenance documentation and SBOM
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: Software developers and suppliers selling to the Federal Government. Broadly adopted as industry best practice.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: NIST published SP 800-218 (SSDF v1.1). OMB M-22-18 and M-23-16 mandate compliance.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Consumer Labeling Programs for IoT and Software
supply_chain_regulations.description: Directs NIST to initiate pilot programs for cybersecurity labeling of consumer IoT devices and software, similar to Energy Star ratings. The labeling program would allow consumers to compare the cybersecurity properties of products, creating market incentives for improved security. For software, labeling criteria include adherence to secure development practices, SBOM availability, and vulnerability management processes.
requirements: NIST to develop IoT cybersecurity labeling criteria
NIST to develop software cybersecurity labeling criteria
Labeling based on secure development practices and transparency
Criteria include SBOM availability and vulnerability management
Pilot programs to evaluate labeling effectiveness
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: Consumer IoT devices and consumer-facing software. Initial focus on pilot programs.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: Voluntary labeling program. FCC launched U.S. Cyber Trust Mark program for IoT in 2024.

supply_chain_regulations.title: Software Source Code Security
supply_chain_regulations.description: Requires NIST guidelines to address security practices for source code management, including automated testing, code review, and the use of source code analysis tools. Emphasizes the importance of securing the development environment and preventing unauthorized modifications to source code. This provision directly supports supply chain integrity by ensuring the source code that enters the build pipeline has not been tampered with.
requirements: Employ automated tools for source code vulnerability analysis
Implement code review processes for security-relevant changes
Secure source code repositories with access controls and audit logging
Maintain integrity of source code throughout the development lifecycle
Test software using automated tools including SAST, DAST, and fuzzing
supply_chain_regulations.applicability: All software producers supplying to the Federal Government.
supply_chain_regulations.enforcement: NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF) practices PW.5, PW.6, PW.7, PW.8. Self-attestation required.
